# AI Is Making Execution Cheap. Judgment Is Becoming the Marketing Moat.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/judgment-is-the-moat/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-31 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: AI has made marketing output fast and cheap, and most B2B teams now use it to create content under pressure to produce more. Volume is no longer a differentiator. The advantage moves to judgment: choosing the problem, checking the claims, keeping an accountable person on consequential decisions, and measuring what changed rather than what shipped.

A team can now produce a month's worth of posts, landing-page drafts and campaign ideas in an afternoon. If nobody has decided who the work is for or what it needs to accomplish, faster production does not solve much. In the Content Marketing Institute's 2026 survey, 88% of B2B marketers said their organisation uses AI content tools and 65% faced more pressure to produce content faster. When everyone can produce, knowing what is worth publishing, and checking whether it worked, is the advantage.

This is a useful distinction for companies buying AI marketing tools or hiring people to use them. Producing the material is getting easier. Knowing *what is worth publishing* remains difficult. Our task-by-task review of [AI agents in marketing](https://lowob.com/research/ai-agents-in-marketing-what-they-can-do-now/) covers what the tools can do; this piece is about what they cannot decide.

## More output isn't the same as better marketing

AI can turn a founder interview into a blog post, a newsletter, a series of social updates and a set of sales messages. It can summarise competitors, suggest headlines and help a small team do work that previously required several specialists. Those are real advantages.

But they only help when the underlying idea is worth communicating. The Content Marketing Institute and MarketingProfs surveyed 861 B2B marketers between June and August 2026. 88% said their organisation uses AI-powered content creation tools, and 60% of those had expanded their use in the past year. 65% said they faced more pressure to produce content faster. The most cited AI content problems were ensuring accuracy and maintaining quality control, each at 54%, and maintaining brand voice at 52%. This is a self-reported survey, not proof that more content made those businesses more successful.

The wider evidence on AI value points the same way. McKinsey's 2025 global survey found 88% of organisations using AI in at least one function, but only 39% attributing any enterprise-level EBIT impact to it, mostly under 5%. The minority that reported significant value were nearly three times as likely to have redesigned workflows, and more likely to have defined when model outputs need human validation. Adoption is common. Results follow from how the work is organised.

When so many teams can produce the same kinds of material, the number of articles or social posts published is a poor measure of whether the marketing is doing its job. Our piece [AI made average marketing cheaper](https://lowob.com/research/ai-made-average-marketing-cheaper/) makes the same point about quality.

> A team that knows when not to publish has an advantage over one that treats every draft as an asset.

## What judgment looks like in an actual project

Imagine a DeFi app whose website attracts visitors but whose wallet-connection numbers barely move. An AI assistant can suggest dozens of campaigns about the product's yield, its security and the size of the market. It cannot settle the basic question on its own: **are people confused by the message, or is the product itself difficult to use?**

The first useful move is to look at the experience. Where do visitors leave? Can they tell what happens after connecting a wallet? Do the people the company hopes to reach actually trust the product? If the problem is an unclear deposit process, commissioning more promotional content is unlikely to fix it.

This example is hypothetical, but the distinction is practical. Choosing the next piece of content depends on knowing what is stopping customers, not just on having a tool capable of writing it.

Good marketing judgment is often a sequence of ordinary decisions: choose one audience, understand what it needs to believe, test whether your claims are supportable, and decide which work deserves time or money. The final output comes after that thinking, not instead of it. [Content with a job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/) turns that sequence into a one-page brief.

## Give AI a clear job, and keep people responsible for the decisions

AI is most useful when a team can tell whether its work is right. Those tasks are easier to review because the underlying information is available.

| Task | Can the team check it? | Who decides |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Organise interview notes or call transcripts | Yes, against the source | AI prepares, a person reviews |
| Compare drafts with approved product facts | Yes, against the fact sheet | AI flags, a person corrects |
| Summarise objections from sales calls | Yes, against the calls | AI drafts, a person confirms |
| Prepare variants of a message already chosen for testing | Yes, against the brief | AI drafts, a person approves |
| Make claims about safety, reliability or performance | Only with specialist knowledge | A named expert, before publication |
| Choose the audience, the budget or the position | Not by the model | An accountable person |

It is less sensible to let a polished draft quietly become the company's position. A model can produce convincing claims about a protocol's safety, an AI product's reliability or a fintech service's advantages without knowing whether the company can substantiate them. Even specialist tools built on retrieval get this wrong: Stanford researchers found leading legal research products gave incorrect information in more than 17% of benchmark queries in 2024. Someone with the relevant knowledge still needs to check the claims before they are published.

The stakes have risen because buyers increasingly read without a seller present. Gartner's March 2026 survey of 646 B2B buyers found 67% preferred a rep-free buying experience and 45% had used AI during a recent purchase. Its analyst noted that sellers "can't rely on static collateral to carry influence in those moments". A wrong claim in published content now travels further, and gets summarised by someone else's model.

**Use AI to prepare.** Gather notes, organise information, explore possible explanations and make first drafts that people can inspect.

**Use evidence to choose.** Look at customer questions, product use, sales objections and campaign results before deciding what deserves attention.

**Keep someone accountable.** Name the person who approves the claim, the audience, the budget and the final published work.

## Measure whether the decision helped

Suppose the DeFi app decides to replace five generic awareness posts with one explanation of the deposit process. The useful measure isn't that the article was delivered quickly. It's whether people who read it understand the product better and complete the next step more often. The team should also check whether any improvement was caused by a product change or a different audience, not assume the article deserves all the credit. [Campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) covers how to set that test up.

| Business | Activity measure (weak) | Outcome measure (stronger) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Consumer DeFi app (illustrative) | Posts published | Readers who complete a deposit |
| Infrastructure sold to businesses | Articles shipped | Fewer confused sales calls; more conversations with the right buyers |
| Developer product | Docs pages added | Successful integrations |

The measures should follow the commercial problem.

More AI-assisted work can be good. More unnecessary work is still unnecessary. A team that knows when *not* to publish has an advantage over one that treats every draft as an asset.

## lowob takeaways

- **Start with the problem, not the prompt.** Know whom you're trying to help and what is currently stopping them.
- **Let AI speed up work you can evaluate.** Research summaries and drafts are useful when someone can verify the result.
- **Keep consequential decisions with an accountable person.** Product claims, audience priorities and budget choices need real context and ownership.
- **Judge the work by what changed.** Published assets are evidence of activity; customer understanding and valuable actions tell you more about effectiveness.

## Common questions

### How many marketers use AI to create content?

Most. In the Content Marketing Institute's 2026 survey of 861 B2B marketers, 88% said their organisation uses AI-powered content creation tools, and 65% reported more pressure to produce content faster.

### What marketing work should AI do, and what should people do?

Give AI work the team can check: organising notes, comparing drafts with approved facts, summarising objections and preparing variants. Keep claims, audience choice, budget and final approval with a named person.

### Does publishing more AI content improve marketing results?

Not by itself. Surveys show volume rising, but not that the extra content improved results. Measure outcomes such as completed next steps or fewer confused sales calls instead of output.

### Who should approve AI-generated marketing claims?

Someone with the relevant product, legal or technical knowledge, named in advance. A model can write convincing claims the company cannot substantiate.

Before commissioning another batch of content, write down what you want customers to understand or do differently, and the measure that will show it happened. Name the person who will approve the claims.
